newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-No cartel call as coffee rally hits consumers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-No cartel call as coffee rally hits consumers.

text.p: A blistering speculative rally in world coffee has now lifted one signal U.S. futures contract to its highest in 20 years.

A volatile mix of low stocks, tight Latin American supply and worries about that Brazil may have another frost has lured a wave of speculative money to the coffee futures markets that determine world prices.
Thursday saw spot May futures for arabica beans trade at $2.79 cents per pound in New York, the highest since June 1977.

The French were on Friday the latest among consumers to be stung by new price rises in the shops. And coffee-growing nations prepared for London talks next week afraid that people may baulk at paying more and turn to tea or soft drinks instead.
Indonesia, the number three seller, said that the producers led by Brazil should show that "we are not a cartel".

Latest increases on retail coffee in France mean that top quality beans there are up by between a third and 45 percent since 1997 began. Shop prices are also up elsewhere in Europe and in the United States.
"Stocks are very very tight", said Pascal Jouannet, chairman of Douwe Egberts France, the French unit of the big Dutch coffee roaster, explaining how the market has soared.
"All supplies are in the hands of origin countries. We are now entering the period when everyone is watching for possible frost in Brazil".

On the spot May futures price, analysts said the spot month was not truly representative. But the July contract - on which there is most interest - is also dramatically up, by almost 125 percent this year at $2.55.
Less-prized robusta coffee beans from Asia and Africa, used in soluble and instant blends, are in more generous supply.
Even so, robusta futures that are traded in London topped $2,000 per tonne on Friday for the first time in a year. That marked a jump of 65 percent since the beginning of 1997.
Shop prices have been edging steadily up in reaction to the longest sustained rally in two decades.
Douwe Egberts, owned by Sara Lee Corp, said this year's French retail increases on its arabica coffees now totalled around 45 percent. Shop prices for robustas were up by 15.

French Cafes Excella SA said on Friday that it planned to further raise retail prices in June. Marketing director Jean-Jacques Dothee told Reuters he did not believe that volatile futures reflected fundamentals of supply and demand.
"There is no risk of a coffee shortage. We are being held hostage by a speculative game..." he said.
Dothee expects prices of some washed Latin American arabicas to stay high until year-end. But other coffees might ease in autumn, provided there was no frost in Brazil.
Dothee also gave a warning that high prices might scare away consumers, notably young people switching to soft drinks.
In 1994-1995 French roasters passed on the cost of higher futures and consumption fell by seven percent. It rebounded by three percent in 1996 when prices went down, he said.
Concerns that high prices may depress demand for coffee will be aired in London next week at talks among 62 producing and consumer nations within the International Coffee Organization.

At parallel sessions, growers in their 14-nation Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) are likely to defer plans to extend export quotas that were designed to keep a floor under world prices when these sagged last year.
"We should demonstrate that we are not a cartel by taking into account the interest of consumers," said Paian Nainggolan of Indonesia, the number three seller after Brazil and Colombia.
The ACPC is to review a 12-month programme that expires on June 30. It had aimed at capping exports at 25.48 million (60 kg) bags in the first half of 1997.
In January, members cut exports by 1.3 million bags, but at a later meeting put some 500,000 bags back on the market.
